Two-tiwr border fencing 
*662.       SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL:† 
DR. T. SUBBARAMi REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has become the third country after Israel and US to 
erect a two-tier border fencing, when proved to be a highlight of the armed 
forces determination to deal with terrorism during 2004; 
(b) whether this two-tier fencing has also helped in reducing the terrorist 
activities in States where insurgency was on increase; 
(c) if so, what are the other steps Gove rnment propose to take to check 
infiltration from Pakistan and Bangladesh; and 
(d) whether the fencing of the border with these countries have been 
fully completed? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the house by Shrimati jamuna 
Devi Barupal. 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) to (c): A double-row fencing is being erected along Indo-Pak and 
Indo-Bangladesh Borders to prevent the trans-border movement of terrorists/ 
infiltrators and other trans-border criminals. Flood lighting has also been 
provided along the fen ce on the Indo-Pak Border and in West Bengal 
Sector of the Indo-Bangladesh Border. In addition, the following steps have 
also been taken to prevent infiltration:— 
(i) Enhancing the force level on the border; 
(ii) Setting up of new BOPs; 
(iii) Round the clock surveillance of the border by carring out 
patrolling, laying nakas and by deploying observation posts all 
along the borders; 
(iv) Upgradation of intelligence network; 
(v) Induction of surveillance equipment and night vision devices. 
(d) No, Sir.

SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: Sir, I wish to know from the hon. Minister 
whether suitable lessons have been drawn from the working of POTA and 
ultimately, its consequent repeal. In other words, has entrusting higher 
powers to the Police, particularly, of making admissible confessions 
recorded by the Police, only increased third-degree torture at the Police 
Stations, without improving the intelligence and efficiency of any 
investigation, or not? 
Secondly, what is it that you are doing now to impart new technology 
and bring in new methods to streamline the processes of investigation? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATlL: Sir, ye sterday we discussed the Malimath 
Committee's Report and this point also came up for discussion. Two or 
three days back, we discussed amen dment to the Criminal Procedure 
Code also. In the Report, and also in POTA, there were suggestions and 
provisions made under which confessions could be recorded by the Police, 
and that confession was made admissible in the court of law. But we have 
repealed POTA, realising that the confession to the Police should not be 
admissible in the court of law. 
While discussing the Malimath Committee's Report yesterday, too, I 
had specifically said that the confession, which is made to the Police, 
should not be treated as evidence and should not be admissible in the 
court of law. That is the stand we have taken. 
We do realise that we shall have to make the criminal laws more humane. 
That is why we have amended the Criminal Procedure Code and we have 
provided some salutary features in that. 
The intent of the question, which has been asked just now, is to see 
that the laws are used in a proper, just and humane manner. That is our

Premier's visit, the Prime Ministers agreed to appoint a Joint Task Force

through non-conventional energy sources in the country; if so, the State-

(b) the projects and schemes are currently in action; and 
(c) the funds allocated for it in the current budget? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON- 
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCE S (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) The potential from non-conventional energy sources such as wind, 
small hydro and bio-energy has been estimated at around 80,000 MW, 
which includes 45000 MW from wind, 15000 MW from small hydro, 19,500 
MW from biomass and 2700 MW from waste to energy. In addition, the 
estimated solar potential is 20 MW/square kilometre. Against this 
estimated potential, 6,160 MW installed capacity for grid interactive 
renewable electricity has been set up, as on 31.03.2005. The aim is to 
deploy around 10 per cent of the additional installed capacity for grid 
interactive electricity from renewables during the Tenth and Eleventh Plan 
periods. However, during the first 3 years, i.e., 2002-03 to 2004-05, of 
the Tenth Plan as much as 18per cent of the additional installed capacity 
has come through renewables, of which the contribution from wind is 
13 per cent (1968 MW), small hydro 2 per cent (267MW), and bio- 
energy 3 per cent (407 MW). A target of 760 MW capacity addition from 
grid interactive renewable electricity  has been set for 2005-05. State- 
wise details of estimated potential from non-conventional energy sources 
and cumulative achievements under grid interactive renewable electricity, 
as on 31.03.2005 are given in Statement-I (See below). 
(b) The details of schemes/programmes of the Ministry of Non- 
conventional Energy Sources for supporting deployment of renewable 
energy systems/devices, given therei n the level of central financial 
assistance are given in Statement-ll (See below). 
(c) There is a Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) of Rs. 600 crore for 
2005-06 for this Ministry. Detailed programme-wise break-down of this

New policy on jute 
*668. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government is considering to bring out a 
new policy on jute. 
(b) If so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Gove rnment are considering to set up a 
National Jute Board; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKER SINH VAGHELA): 
(a) and (b) Yes Sir. Government has announced the National Jute Policy 
2005 of India on 15th April 2005. The objectives of the policy are to 
increase the quantity of export of jute and jute products by achieving a 
CAGR of 15% per annum, produce good quality jute fibre and value 
added diversified jute products, ensure remunerative prices to the jute 
farmers. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
The specific sectoral thrusts to achieve the aforesaid objectives are to; 
1. Enhance R&D efforts to improve yield and quality of jute fibre 
along with improved emphasis on technology transfer and better 
agronomic practices. 
2. Accelerate Modernization of the jute industry. 
3. Restructure and revitalise the existing Public Sector 
Undertakings. 
4. Revamp the Market Support Sche me to enhance the share of 
exports in total production of jute goods from existing 18% to 
35% in next 10 years. 
5. Achieve higher degree of jute diversification through enhanced 
efforts in R&D by establishing a Jute R&D fund, a Venture Capital 
Assistance Fund, and a full fledge d Design and Development Cen- 
tre. 
6. Restructure and revamp existing public institutions and establish 
new ones to give a fresh impetus to the jute sector. This includes 
establishment of a Jute Board. The Government is also contem- 
plating the establishment of a National Institute of Natural Fibres 
and a National Jute and Jute Textile Museum. 
7. Operationalise the Jute Technology Mission. 
(c) and (d) A National Jute Board will be set up to rectify the systemic 
ills of lack of coordination among th e several jute related organizations 
under different Ministries and Departments of the Government, and to 
synchronise and synergise the integrated development of the jute sector 
as a whole. This is necessary to synthesize the various layers of 
Governmental decision-making in a federal set up. This body will subsume, 
merge, and integrate the functions of va rious institutions currently operating 
in the jute sector. The mandate of the proposed Jute Board will be as 
follows: 
(i) To restructure the present regulatory framework so as to provide 
adequate incentive to all stakeholders in the jute sector to produce 
38 

[11 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
goods and services in an efficient manner so as to maximize 
socio-economic benefits. 
(ii) To subsume and revamp the office of the Jute Commissioner and 
transform it from an office of regulation to a facilitator of development 
in the jute sector. 
(iii) To establish a Jute R&D fund and Venture capital assistance 
fund for the development of efficient jute manufacturing machinery, 
and the commercialization of new products; 
(iv) To strengthen and facilitate the growth of HRD institutions like the 
Institute of Jute Technology (IJT) on innovative-lines. 
(v) To review and revitalise the working of the R&D institutions like 
the Indian Jute Industries Research Association (IJIRA) to focus 
research on industry needs. 
(vi) To subsume, merge and professionalise field organisations like 
Jute Manufacture Development Coun cil (JMDC) and the National 
Centre for Jute Diversification (NCJD) under the Ministry of Textiles 
to enable them to play their assign ed role of facilitators of change 
and growth effectively. 
(vii) To explore the possibility of establishing a National Institute of 
Natural Fibres with the objective of harmonizing developmental 
and promotional activities pertaini ng to all natural fibres, and to 
have a better sharing of experience and knowledge in related 
fibres. 
(viii) To establish a National Jute a nd Jute Textile Museum in India to 
preserve and highlight the heritage of jute. 
Subsidiary institutions functioning under the aegis of the Ministry of 
Agriculture under Department of Agricultural Research & Education (DARE/ 
ICAR) like National Institute for Research on Jute & Allied Fibre Technology 
(NIRJAFT), and the Central Research In stitute for Jute and Allied Fibres 
(CRIJAF) will be integrated with the Ju te Board in a meaningful relationship, 
as also the functions and issues presently being administrated by the 
Ministry of Agriculture.

Crime on Railways 
*678. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of incidents of crime on Railways during the last three 
years; 
(b) whether such incidents have increased; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps taken to check incidents of crime on Railways? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANIKRAO HODLYAGAVIT): (a) to (c) As per information furnished 
by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), the incidents of crime on 
Railways have shown a mixed trend in the case of dacoities while a de- 
clining trend is observed with respect to incidents of burglary and thefts 
during 2001-2003. The provisional figures of 2004 as compared to 2003 
indicate a decline of 17.9% in dacoity  cases, 45% in robbery cases and 
86.1 % in burglary cases. The details of incidents of dacoity, robbery, bur- 
glary and theft on Railways during 2001 to 2004 is given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(d) Government has taken the following steps for providing better 
security to the travelling passengers in trains and passenger 
areas: 
(i) Amendments have been carried out in Railways Act, 1989 and 
RPF Act, 1957 to enable the Railways to effectively control crimes 
on Railways. 
60 

[11 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Railway Protection Force (RPF) is being deployed to escort many 
trains and also deployed in the passenger area. 
(iii) RPF has also been empowered to deal with minor offences 
affecting the train operations such as alarm chain pulling, 
roof travel, touting, ticket less travel, unauthorised entry 
etc.; 
(iv) Coordination meetings between Railways and State police are 
held periodically to review remedial measures for prevention of 
crimes on Railways, the position in the sections, trains and sta- 
tions affected by crime. 
(v) Whenever there is a flare-up of violent incidents in any section, 
all-out efforts are made in co-ordination with the State police to 
control the situation, by actively assisting them with additional 
manpower and other resources. 
(vi) From July 2004, after amendment of RPF Act, out of its total 
sanctioned strength of 66,170, whic h includes 658 lady constables, 
Railway Protection Force is providing on an average of 1,134 es- 
cort parties per day in affected trains, in co-ordination with the 
State Governments, for which an average of 3,431 staff are de- 
ployed. 
(vi) 557 stations, on an average are being provided security by RPF 
with deployment of approximately 3,008 personnel daily. These 
deployments are in addition to 2103 Government Railway Police 
(GRP) personnel deployed on trains  and 4863 personnel deployed 
on the railway premises. 
(viii) 3237 trains are being escorted by either Railway Protection Force 
(RPF) or Government Railway Police (GRP).

Steps to revive jute industry 
*679. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARAYA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is considering a proposal to infuse fresh life in 
the dying jute industry. 
(b) if so, the details of the proposal under consideration; 
(c) whether the six ailing jute mills in West Bengal are being proposed 
to be revived under the new dispensation and if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether there is a provision also for the modernisation and 
upgradation of the jute mills and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILE (SHRI SHANKERSiNGH VAGHELA): (a) 
and (b) In order to give a fresh impetus to the jute industry in all respects, 
Government of India announced the National Jute Policy, 2005 on 15th 
April 2005. The policy retails sectoral  initiatives that will be taken to 
modernize the jute industry and make it competitive. These sectoral ob- 
jectives will cover the cultivation of ju te, the modernization of the industry, 
marketing, organizational restructuring in the public sector and human 
resource development and labour welfare. In addition, a Jute Technology 
Mission will also be operationalised. The emphasis of the Jute Policy will 
be to position all jute and allied fibres as superior and environmental friendly 
material, check the erosion of the market for traditional fibres and encour- 
age diversification. The export sector will be encouraged to increase the 
export of diversified jute products through innovative marketing strategies 
and improvement of product design. 
(c) The National Jute Police, 2005 stat es thet efforts would be made to 
restructure and revitalise the existing Public Sector Undertakings. The 
Government has recently approved a plan of action for the mills under the 
National Jute Manufactures Corporation (NJMC) which includes the grant 
of benefits under a Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) to all the employ- 
ees, and extending budgetary support for providing VRS, liquidating statu- 
tory arrears, gratuity, and the secured liabilities of the company. The 
Government will initiate steps to review the Khardah and Kinnison units of 
NJMC ltd. 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
(d) The National Jute Policy, 2005 envisages concerted efforts for the 
modernisation and technology upgradation of the manufacturing sector. 
This will include i) re-orientation of manufacture of jute goods as per cur- 
rent international requirements while addressing the issues of quality and 
cost competitiveness, ii) energizing the jute yarn and twine making sector 
in view of the rise in demand for jute diversified products, iii) adopting 
environmental friendly manufacturing processes, and iv) augmenting the 
research and development efforts to commercialise jute technical textiles 
including geo-textiles. The existing schemes like the Technology 
Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) and the Jute Manufaturers Develop- 
ment Council (JMDC) incentive scheme  for the modernisation of the jute 
"industry will be strengthened.

Agricultural exports 
 †5141. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
DR. MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the agricultural products of India have to 
compete with that of developed countries in international market under 
free trade market under WTO; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that subsidy upto 300 billion dollars per 
year is being provided for exports of agricultural products in developed 
countries; 
(c) if so, the facts thereof; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the above-said crisis would continue to 
be faced by Indian agro-products for the next five years following the recent 
Delhi Declaration of G-21 Nations; and 
(e) if so, the steps being taken by Government to deal with this crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (c) The international 
trading environment for agricultural products is governed by the inter-play 
of multilateral rules and disciplines embodied in the Marrakesh Agree- 
ment Establishing the World Trade Organisation (WTO Agreement) which 
apply to developed and developing Members alike, regional and bilateral 
arrangements, as well as domestic pol icies, constraints and capacities. 
Furthermore, fully recognizing that the long-term objective of the WTO's 
Agreement on Agriculture is to establish a "fair and market-oriented" agri- 
cultural trading system, Article 20 of this Agreement has a built-in man- 
date to continue the reform process to reduce support and protection 
provided by Member governments. A free trade market for agricultural prod- 
ucts thus is not yet established by the AoA, but developed and developing 
countries compete with each other respecting their present commitments 
scheduled by them under the WTO for various agricultural products. In the 
on-going negotiations, there is explicit recognition that the huge amounts 
of support, subsidies and protection provided to their farm sector by many 
developed Members distort world agricultural trade and are not equitious 
 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
given that most developing countries do not have the requisite financial 
resources to extend comparable levels of support to their farmers. As per 
an OECD report, support to agriculture in OECD countries totalled US $ 
361 billion in 1999, and has hovered around this level since then also. 
(d) and (e) The G-20 Ministerial D eclaration, New Delhi, contains a 
proposal to eliminate all forms of ex port subsidies in five years, with a 
front-loading of commitments. If the proposal is agreed at the WTO, the 
export subsidies will be get reduced substantially from the very first year 
itself and totally eliminated in a period of five years thereby increasing the 
market access opportunities for the agri cultural products of developing 
countries through this period as well. No other timelines have been set out 
in the Declaration. The period for implementation of commitments across 
all the three pillars (domestic support, export competition and market 
access) will be a part of the agr eement to be reached among all WTO 
Members in the on-going negotiations under the Doha Work Programme. 
The Government is making all efforts by building coalitions with like minded 
countries and is working within alliances such as the G-20 and the G-33 
to ensure that our objectives are achieved.

has an allocation of 162 MW from unallocated quota of CGSs in WR as

Generation of power from 
hydro electric sector 
5230. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether in the recent years pow er generation from hydro electric 
sector has decreased; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor, and 
(c) the steps taken to increase power from hydro electric sector? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) 
Production of electricity from hydro power stations depends on water 
availability/inflow which in turn depends on the extent of rainfall in the 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
catchment areas as also the snowfall for power stations on the snow-fed 
Himalayan rivers. In case of hydro electric power stations on some of the 
rivers in Central and Southern Regions, the progressive decline in water 
availability results from upstream multipurpose utilization of water. The 
aspect of the variation in water availability at hydro electric power stations 
is taken into consideration at the planning/design stage of power stations. 
The low water availability was experienced during the last few years due 
to poor monsoons in the country as also lesser snowfall during the year 
2003-04. 
The trend in generation from hydro electric power stations in the country 
during recent years was mixed. Region-wise/AII India hydro generation for 
last three years i.e. 2002-03 to 2004-05 is given in the Statement (See 
below). 
(c) Based on the Ranking Studies made in 2001-02 by the Central 
Electricity Authority (CEA), 50,000 MW hydro electric initiative was launched 
by Government of India during 2003-04 under which Pre-Feasibility Reports 
(PFRs) of 162 schemes located in 16 States have been prepared. Based 
on preliminary analysis, 78 schemes a ggregating to an installed capacity 
of 34,020 MW, whose first year tariff works out at Rs. 2.50/KwH or below, 
have been identified for taking up detailed Survey and Investigation and 
preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). 
In addition to above, the Government has taken the following steps to 
harness the untapped hydro potential: 
(i) A Hydro Policy was announced by the Government in August, 1998 
incorporating several steps and measures to facilitate accelerated 
development of hydro power. The Policy also encourages greater 
participation by private sector. 
(ii) A number of Hydro Power Corporations in the Central Sector and 
Joint Ventures with State Governments have been created for 
development of hydro power. 
(iii) The Government has also approved a Three-Stage Clearance 
procedure for expeditious execution of hydro electric projects in the 
Central Sector including procedural reforms.

Area Development Programmes namely, the Integrated Wastelands 
Development Programme (IWDP), the Drought Prone Areas Programme 
(DPAP) and the Desert Development Programme (DDP) for treatment 
of non-forest wastelands/degraded la nds on watershed approach. DPAP 
and DDP are being implemented in the identified blocks of the country 
whereas IWDP is being implemente d in the non-DPAP/DDP areas of

implemented in all the States of th e country. DPAP and DDP are being

in the country.

DPAP, 1224 projects have been sanctioned to identified blocks of 16 districts 
in Tamil Nadu covering an area of 6. 12 lakh hectares at a total cost of

India as a textile hub 
5252. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India will emerge as textile hub for the 
European Union and the United States by 2014; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the country needs to expand its activities 
if we have to encash the opportunities available in textile sector; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. According to variou s studies, China and India will carve 
out a larger share of EU and US markets in the post quota regime. India's 
growth in exports will be  driven by value added made ups and apparel as 
India has comparative advantages over its competitors in relation to (i) 
availability of relatively inexpensive and skilled workforce (ii) design 
expertise (iii) large production base of basic raw material like home grown 
cotton, yarns and fabrics and (iv) availability of wide range of textiles. 
According to a study by CRISIL (on behalf of Indian Cotton Mills 
Federation), the Indian textiles and apparel industry has a potential to 
double the country's share of the global textiles and clothing market, 
implying export earning of US$ 40 billion by 2010- In order to achieve the 
full potential, investment of Rs. 1,40,000 crore would be required, not only 
to modernise existing capacities but also to create fresh capacity. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Government has been taking a number of steps 
from time to time to promote investments in the textile sector and thereby 
increase India's textile exports. Some  of the important initiatives taken 
are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(ii) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The Mission 
comprises for mini-missions, which are being jointly implemented 
206 

[11 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
by the Ministry of Agricultural and Ministry of Textiles. One of the 
important ingredients of the Mission is to improve cotton processing 
facilities by upgrading/modernizing the existing griming and pressing 
facilities and setting up of new market yards/improvement of existing 
market yards. 
(iii) The Government has launched a centrally sponsored scheme titled 
"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for 
setting up of apparel manufacturing units of international standards 
as potential growth centres to give fillip to exports. 
(iv) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, a 
scheme titled 'Textile Centre Infr astructure Development Scheme" 
(TCIDS) has been launched. 
(v) The fiscal duty structure has been generally raationalised to achieve 
growth and maximum value addition within the country. Except for 
mandatory excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-made 
staple fibres, the wholevalue addition chain has been given excise 
exemption option. 
(vi) The important of specified textiles and garmet machinery items has 
been allowed at concessional ra te of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile  products competitive in the global 
market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal 
policy measures. 
(vi) Duty-free imports of 21 items of trimmings and embellishment items 
are allowed to the garment exporters, upto 3% of their actual export 
performance during the previous year. 
(vi) National Institute for Fashion Te chnology (NIFT), its seven branches 
and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing. 
(ix) Facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories have been created to 
enable exporters to get the garments/textiles pre-tested for conforming 
to the requirements of importing countries. 
207 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
(x) The Government has de-reserved the radyrnade garments, hoisery 
and knitwear from the SSI sector.

5253. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Mi nister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently some fresh initiatives have been 
taken for the development ana growth of the jute industry; and for inter-alia 
achieving a five fold increase in export over the next five years to Rs. 5,000 
crores, against the current level of Rs. 1,000 crores;

upgradation and incentives proposed tor achieving the higher export targets 
by the industry; and

2005 on 15.04.2005 in order to achieve the overall development and growth 
of the jute industry. One of the objec tives of the Policy is to increase the 
exports to Rs. 5000 crores by 2010 from the current level of Rs. 1000 
crores. 
2. With the objective in view: 
(0 A multi-disciplinary institutional mechanism will be established to 
formulate policy measres and speci fic action plans, including those 
relating to the WTO, and for closely monitoring financial proposals; 
(ii) Strategic alliances will be forg ed with an aim to gain access to

(iii) A brand equity fund, exclusively fo r jute and jute products will be set

208 

[11 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) The proposed Jute Board will incorporate an Export Promotion Council 
which will play the role of facilitator and professional consultant for 
dealing with disputes under va rious agreements of the WTO, 
establishing warehousing facilities in major jute and jute product 
importing countries and identifying the existing patent issues with a 
view to patenting India R&D efforts. 
3. The programme for the modernisation and technological upgradation 
of the manufacturing sector will includ e (i) re-orientation of manufacture of 
jute goods as per current International requirements while addressing the

and twine making sector in view of the rise in demand for jute diversified 
products, (iii) adopting environmental friendly manufacturing processes 
and (iv) augmenting the research and development efforts to commercialise 
jute technical textiles including geo-textiles. The existing schemes like 
the Technology Upgradation Fund Schemes (TUFS) and the Jute 
Manufacturer's Development Council (JMDC) incentive scheme for the 
modernisation of the Jute Industry will be strengthened.

India as a major textile exporter 
5256. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA. Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India, along with China will become a major 
textile exporter in the world after the Multi Fibre Agreement ended on

(b) how the Ministry justifies the view of experts that India is expected 
to grow at the rate of 250 per cent in the next five years in textiles in the 
light of removal of QRs; and 
(c) what avenues that the GOI is giving to the textile ancillary firms of 
other countries so as to establish themselves in the Indian market? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
As per WTO Agreement on Textiles an d Clothing (ATC), the textile quota 
regime has been phased out and textile sector fully integrated into WTO 
211

on 1st January, 2005. According to various international studies, China

regime. The foreign buyers who are heavily dependent on China are also

by Pakistan) to ensure growth of their business.

dismantling of the quota system and the consequent opening up of the

competitive advantages resulting from labour, technology and raw materials.

potential to achieve a CAGR of 21 %.

Sir, as hon. Members are aware, the Prevention of Money-Laundering 
 
†Transliteration in Urdu Script. 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
Act, 2002 was enacted to prevent money-laundering and to provide for 
confiscation of property derived from, or, involved in money-laundering. 
The enactment of this Act had become necessary to implement the political 
declaration adopted by the Special Sessi on of the United Nations General 
Assembly held in June, 1999 which called upon Member-States to adopt 
national money-laundering legislation and programme. The Act stipulates 
that it shall come into force on such  date as the Central Government may 
notify. While examining the Act before notifying, I found that there were 
certain lacunae and these lacunae made it  difficult to notify the Act. Under 
Section 45 of the Act, every offence punishable under the Act is made 
cognizable. By virtue of the definition of 'cogniza ble' in the Criminal 
Procedure Code, any Police Officer can arrest an offender without a warrant. 
At the same time, under Section 19 of the Act, the Director, the Deputy 
Director, the Assistant Director, or, an y other officer authorised, can arrest 
an offender. Therefore, in the Act, there are two sets of officers; the officers 
named in the Act and the regular Police Officers who can exercise the 
powers of arrest. However, under the se cond proviso to Section 45 (1) (b), 
the special court can take cogniz ance of an offence punishable under 
Section 4 only upon a complaint, in writ ing, made by the Director, or, any 
officer authorised by the Central Government. So, obviously, these provisions 
were in conflict with each other. T he question arose as to what would 
happen to a person arrested by a regu lar Police Officer in a regular Police 
Station. Now, through amendments under Sections 44 and 45, we have 
made the offences non-cognizable. Once  the PMLA comes into force, we 
will prescribe a threshold limit, below which we will authorise any Police 
Officer to take action. In all other case s, that is, cases above the threshold 
limit, the powers will vest in the Direc tor, or, any officer authorised by him. 
This will bring the provisions consist ent with Section 45(1 )(b). The second 
shortcoming that we noticed was that  expressions "investigation" and 
"investigating officer", which occur in a number of Sections, had not been 
defined. The definition h ad, therefore, to be der ived from the Criminal 
Procedure Code, which provides for inve stigation only by a Police Officer, 
or, by any person who is authorised by a magistrate in this behalf. 
So, the question arose how will the Director or the Deputy Director 
investigate an offence? So, we are curing that lacuna by inserting a definition 
in Section 2. Another difficulty that we came across was a huge expenditure 
involved in setting up a separate Appellate Tribunal under the Act. It is, 
therefore, proposed to uti lise the services of any existing Appellate Tribunal 
by notifying the Chairperson and Members of that Tribunal who possess 
228 

[11 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the qualifications prescribed in the Act as the Chairperson and Members 
of the Tribunal under the PMLA Act also. In order to bring the qualifications 
of the Chairperson of the Tribunal under  PMLA in line with the Chairpersons 
of some other Tribunals, some small amendments are proposed in sections 
28,29 and 30 of the Act. I would like to  assure the House that in proposing 
these amendments, we are not, I repeat, we are not diluting the impact of 
the Act, as new amendments are being  proposed either to section 3, 
which defines an offence, or, section 4 which provides for punishment. 
Those sections remain intact. The only purpose of these amendments is 
to remove the lacunae, make the Act enforceable so that we can notify it 
quickly.

NATH): Sir, I assure that I will satisf y him of all the concerns he has Sir, I 
move: 
"That the Bill to provide for t he establishment, development and 
management of the Special Economic Z ones for the promotion of exports 
and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto as passed by 
Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, the Government of India ha d announced a Special Economic Zone 
Scheme in April 2000 with a view to provide an internationally competitive 
environment for exports. The objectives of Special Economic Zones include 
making available goods and services free of taxes and duties supported 
by an integrated infrastructure for export production, quick approval 
mechanisms, and a package of incentiv es to attract foreign and domestic 
investments for promoting export. 
There are, at present, 11 functioning Special Economic Zones.ln addition, 
approvals have been given for setting up of 35 new Special Economic 
Zones in the private, joint and State sectors. 
283 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2005] 
While the policy relating to the Special Economic Zones is contained in 
the Foreign Trade Policy, incentives and other facilities offered to the Special 
Economic Zone developer and units are implemented through various 
notifications and circulars issued by the concerned Ministries and 
Departments. The present system, th erefore, does not inspire enough 
confidence for investors to commit s ubstantial funds for development of 
infrastructure. To provide a long-term and stable policy framework with a 
minimum regulatory regime and to provide expeditious single-window 
clearance facilities, a Central Act for Special Economic Zones has been 
found to be necessary in line with international practice. 
It is expected that introduction and passage of this Bill will provide 
confidence and stability to domestic and foreign investors and signal the 
Government's commitment to the SE Z policy framework. It is expected 
that many large format, multi-product SEZs that have so far been unable 
to achieve financial closure will now quickly move towards closure. It is 
anticipated that the new law would tri gger a large flow of Foreign Direct 
Investment as well as dom estic investment in infrastructure and productive 
capacity leading to the creation of new employment opportunities. 
Sir, the salient features of the bill are:- 
(i) Matters relating to establishment of Special Economic Zone and for 
setting up of units therein, includi ng requirements, obligaitons and 
entitlements: 
(ii) Matters relating to requirement s for setting up of off-shore banking 
units and units in International Fi nancial Service Centre in Special 
Economic Zones, including the fiscal regime governing the operation 
of such units; 
(iii) The fiscal regime for developer s of Special Economic Zones and 
units set up therein: 
(iv)   Single-window clearance mechanism at the zone level. 
(v) Establishment of an authority fo r each Special Economic Zone set 
up by the Central Government to impart greater administrative 
autonomy; and 
(vi) Designation of special courts  and a single enforcement agency to 
ensure speedy trial and investigation of notified offences committed 
in Special Economic Zones.
